nameStory: The name "landlady's wig" comes from this seaweed's tangled, wiry appearance that resembles an old-fashioned wig that's seen better days. Picture the kind of frazzled hairpiece a stern boarding house keeper might wear in Victorian times - all twisted and disheveled from years of use!
description: Landlady's wig is a red seaweed that forms dense, tangled masses along rocky shores. Despite being called a "red alga," it often appears dark purple, brownish-red, or nearly black when you find it. The plant consists of wiry, rope-like strands that branch and twist together in seemingly chaotic patterns. It typically grows in clumps several inches across, creating dense mats that cling tightly to rocks.

idTips.label: Wiry texture
idTips.description: The branches feel tough and cartilaginous, like thick fishing line or thin rope - much firmer than most other seaweeds you'll encounter

idTips.label: Tangled growth pattern
idTips.description: Forms chaotic, bird's nest-like clumps with branches that twist and interweave irregularly, never growing in neat, orderly patterns

idTips.label: Dark coloration
idTips.description: Usually appears dark reddish-brown to purplish-black, rarely the bright red you might expect from a "red alga"

idTips.label: Cylindrical branches
idTips.description: Individual strands are round in cross-section, not flattened like many seaweeds, and feel smooth when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Strong attachment
idTips.description: Clings very tightly to rocks with a strong holdfast - you'll need to pull hard to remove it, and it often breaks rather than coming free

habitat: Look for landlady's wig in the lower intertidal zone of rocky New England shores, especially where waves crash regularly. It prefers exposed coastlines with good water circulation and attaches to granite ledges, boulders, and rocky crevices. You'll often find it growing alongside other tough seaweeds like rockweed and Irish moss in areas that get pounded by surf.

seasonality.spring: Plants begin active growth as water temperatures rise, with new branches appearing lighter in color than the dark, weathered winter growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when the tangled masses are most prominent and easiest to spot during low tides.
seasonality.fall: Still visible and identifiable, though growth slows as temperatures drop and storm waves may tear away some of the summer's growth.
seasonality.winter: Persists through cold months, appearing darker and more compact, with the toughest, most weathered specimens clinging to rocks through winter storms.

funFact: This humble seaweed is one of the toughest organisms on Earth - it can survive being frozen solid in Arctic ice, then thaw out and continue growing as if nothing happened, making it a true survivor of the harsh North Atlantic.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other dark, stringy seaweeds, but landlady's wig is much tougher and more wiry to the touch - if it feels soft or slimy, you're looking at something else. Remember: "landlady tough, tenant soft" - this seaweed feels as stern as its namesake!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "red alga," don't expect bright red coloration - many red algae are actually brown, purple, or black due to additional pigments that help them photosynthesize in deeper or more turbulent waters where red light doesn't penetrate well.
compareHints: Since landlady's wig is the only Ahnfeltia species in New England waters, compare it to other wiry red seaweeds in the region. Unlike the more delicate branching patterns of most red algae, landlady's wig has that distinctive tough, rope-like texture and chaotic tangled growth that sets it apart. Other red seaweeds in similar habitats tend to be either much softer or grow in more organized, feathery patterns.
